TO THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS

REPLY BRIEF FOR THE PETITIONER


 D. JOHN SAUER
Solicitor General
Counsel of Record
Department of Justice
Washington, D.C. 20530 -0001
SupremeCtBriefs@usdoj.gov
(202) 514 -2217

(1)
In the Supreme Court of the United States

No. 26-104
PHILIP L. RHONEY, ACTING FIELD OFFICE DIRECTOR OF
THE BUFFALO FIELD OFFICE OF U.S. IMMIGRATION AND
CUSTOMS ENFORCEMENT, PETITIONER
v.
RICARDO APARECIDO BARBOSA DA CUNHA

ON PETITION FOR A WRIT OF CERTIORARI
TO THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS
FOR THE SECOND CIRCUIT

REPLY BRIEF FOR THE PETITIONER

This case presents the question whether 8 U.S.C.
1225(b)(2) (A) mandates the detention of aliens  like respondent  who are present in the United States without
having been admitted.  For the reasons given in the petition for a writ of certiorari (at 11-13), this Court should
hold the petition pending the resolution of the petition
in Putra v. Lopez-Campos, petition for cert. pending ,
No. 25 -1415 (filed June 22, 2026) .  In addition to presenting the statutory question at issue in this case,
Lopez-Campos also presents a due-process  challenge to
detention under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) , which the Court
should resolve alongside the statutory question.  See
Pet. 12-13.
Respondent acknowledges that the statutory question presented in this case has divided the courts of appeals, is extremely important , and m erits this Court’s

2

review.  See Cert. Resp. Br.  18.  But he contends  (id. at
18-19) that the Court should resolve that question in a
case that does not separately present the que stion
whether an alien’s detention under Section 1225(b)(2)(A)
comports with due process.  Accordingly, he urges (id.
at 20) the Court to grant  a writ of  certiorari in this case
or in  Buenrostro -Mendez v. Blanche, petition for cert.
pending, No. 26-43 (filed July 2, 2026 ), rather than in
Lopez-Campos.
Respondent’s arguments lack merit.  As the government has explained,  Lopez-Campos is an ideal vehicle
precisely because it presents both the statutory and
the constitutional question .  See Pet. at 32-34, Lopez-
Campos, supra (No. 25-1415) (Lopez-Campos Pet.); Br.
for Fed. Resp.  at 13-14, Buenrostro -Mendez, supra
(No. 26-43) (Buenrostro -Mendez Br.).  The due-process
question is constantly recurring because a liens detained
under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) —including respondent in
this case —overwhelmingly raise it alongside a statutory claim in their habeas petitions .  If this Court were
to grant review of only the statutory question and adopt
the government’s interpretation, district courts around
the country may continue to order bond hearings for
covered aliens on due-process grounds.  See Buenrostro-
Mendez Br. at 14.  Another year could pass before a uniform rule governs the detention of aliens who are present
in this country without being admitted.  See id. at 15.
Moreover, the statutory and due -process issues are
conceptually entwined.  As respondent acknowledges
(at 19), the court of appeals in this case considered due -
process arguments in the context of constitutional
avoidance, as an additional argument for adopting respondent’s interpretation.  See Pet. App. 55a -59a.  Respondent nevertheless denies that the constitutional

3

and statutory challenges to Section 1225(b)(2)(A) detention are necessarily linked,  on the theory that the Second Circuit’s discussion of constitutional avoidance was
“unnecessary” to its ultimate conclusion.   Cert. Resp.
Br. 19.  But it is unclear why respondent would not want
the Court to consider all possible arguments for his preferred interpretation, including constitutional avoidance.  Moreover, even if the parties to the case do not
raise that argument,  amici may put  it before the Court.
Given that the Court may be asked to consider due -process issues in the course of its statutory analysis, it
would be more efficient to grant a petition that squarely
presents both questions and arises from lower -court decisions that thoroughly addressed bo th issues.
Respondent’s remaining arguments for deferring
consideration of the due -process issue lack merit.  Respondent asserts ( at 18) that the due -process issue “ involves no circuit split.”  But this Court regularly grants
review without waiting for a circuit conflict when lower
courts invalidate federal statutes on constitutional
grounds.  See Lopez-Campos Pet. at 32.  Respondent
also urges  (at 18-19) the Court  to wait to decide  Genalo
v. Black, cert. granted, No. 25 -886 ( oral argument
scheduled for Oct. 13, 2026 ), before it takes up a due -
process challenge to Section 1225(b)(2)(A).  That is a difficult position for respondent to maintain now that counsel for the respondent in  Genalo—who are also respondent’s counsel here —have asked this Court to dismiss
that case as moot without reaching the due -process issue.  See Resp. Br. at 20, Genalo, supra (No. 25 -886).
Regardless, there is no reason to defer consideration of
the due -process issue in this case for Genalo.  While
there is conceptual overlap between the issues in the
two cases , they involve due-process challenges to dis-

4

tinct statutory provisions.  See Buenrostro -Mendez Br.
at 16.  Moreover, respondent does not explain why the
Court could not consider both issues during the same
Term.  I ndeed, the Court might find it useful to do so.
See id. at 17.
Because only Lopez-Campos squarely and separately presents the due -process issue, that case is the
best vehicle for this Court’s review.
* * * * *
For the foregoing reasons and those stated  in the petition for a writ of certiorari, the  Court should hold the
petition pending the disposition of the petition in Putra
v. Lopez-Campos, petition for cert. pending, No. 25-1415
(filed June 22, 2026), and should then dispose of this petition as appropriate .
Respectfully submitted.
  D. JOHN SAUER
Solicitor General
SEPTEMBER  2026
